```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE)
```

This walks one stock from a set of input files to numbers and mean weights
at length and age, and says what to put in each argument along the way.

Everything the app does is a call in this vignette. The app adds pickers
and figures; it adds no arithmetic. If a run can be done here it can be
done there, and the app's **R script** tab writes out exactly this
sequence for the session you just ran.

```{r}
library(rcef)
```

## The shape of the thing

```
                     derive_fields()
  input files  ──►  catch_data  ──┬──► build_strata() ──► classify_strata()
                                  │           │
                                  │           ▼                    explore,
                                  │    define_raising_groups_*()   filter,
                                  │           │                    decide
                                  │           ▼
                                  └──► catchRaising()  ──►  catch_raised
                                                                │
                              distributions ────────────────────┤
                                                                ▼
                                                     catchAllocationAoL()
                                                                │
                                       catchAtAoLAggregation()  ▼
                                    meanWoLatAoLAggregation() ──► results
```

Two objects are worth separating in your head from the start:

* **`catch_data`** — every row for the stock and year. This is what gets
  grouped and raised.
* **`explore_data`** — a subset you are *looking* at. This is what gets
  plotted.

They are different on purpose. Filtering to one metier to read a coverage
figure is a normal, good thing to do; raising a stock on one metier
because the filter was still on is not. The package never lets one become
the other silently — see [Exploring](#exploring-with-a-filter).

## 1. Loading the data

Three routes in, depending on what you have. All three end at the same
place: a CEF (RDBES) long-format `catches` table, plus a `distributions`
table if you want length or age work.

### Route A — CEF files you already have

```{r}
catch_data <- read.csv("catches_CEF_v17.1.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
dist_data  <- read.csv("distributions_CEF_v17.1.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
```

### Route B — InterCatch exchange format

One file holding the HI, SI and SD records. `funIntercatchCEF()` reads
*every* csv in the directory it is pointed at, binds them, and splits on
the record-type column — so a single combined export is the normal input.

```{r}
funMakeRelation()          # builds stock_relation; needs icesVocab + icesSD

ic <- funIntercatchCEF(
  dat_path       = "data/intercatch",
  stock_relation = stock_relation,
  output_format  = "to_list")

catch_data <- ic$catches
dist_data  <- ic$distributions
```

| argument | what to put in it |
|---|---|
| `dat_path` | folder holding the exchange file(s). Not a file path — a folder. |
| `stock_relation` | the lookup from `funMakeRelation()`. It also assigns `stock_relation` into the global environment, so passing it explicitly is belt and braces. |
| `output_format` | `"to_list"` for use here. `"to_environment"` assigns into the global env, `"to_file"` writes CEF csvs with headers, `"to_upload"` writes headerless upload files. |
| `out_path` | only meaningful for the two file formats. |

### Route C — InterCatch output format

Three files: `StockOverview`, `NumbersAtAgeLength`, `MeanWeigthAtAgeLength`
(the upstream spelling of the third is preserved — match it).

```{r}
ic <- funICoutCEF(dat_path = "data/ic_output", output_format = "to_list")
catch_data <- ic$catches
dist_data  <- ic$distributions
```

### Then, always

```{r}
catch_data <- derive_fields(catch_data)
```

`derive_fields()` is not optional. It splits the flat CEF columns into the
nested ones everything downstream groups on:

| in | out |
|---|---|
| `areaValue` | `ICESSubArea` (`27.4`), `ICESDivision` (`27.4.b`), `ICESSubdivision` (`27.4.b.1`) |
| `fleetValue` | `metier4` (`TBB`), `metier5`, `metier6`, `target`, `mesh`, `FleetType` |
| `vesselFlagCountry` | `Country` |
| `seasonValue` | `Season` |

A code coarser than the level asked for **repeats** rather than becoming
`NA`: `27.4` is its own division and subdivision as far as the data goes.
That is deliberate — a stratum reported at coarse resolution is never
silently dropped out of a finer grouping.

It needs `fleetValue`, `areaValue`, `vesselFlagCountry` and `seasonValue`
and errors if any is missing, which is the fastest way to find out that a
file is not really CEF.

Finally, scope to one stock and year:

```{r}
catch_data <- subset(catch_data, stock == "sol.27.4" & year == 2023)
```

## 2. Strata

```{r}
dims   <- c("metier4", "Country", "ICESDivision", "Season")
strata <- build_strata(catch_data, dims)
```

`dims` is *the* decision of this step: it is the resolution at which you
will look at coverage and, usually, the resolution at which you will
raise. Four dimensions — fleet, country, area, season — is the habit, but
any subset of the derived columns works.

`build_strata()` returns one row per stratum with:

| column | meaning |
|---|---|
| `landings` | total landings, tonnes |
| `landings_with_discards` | landings in the part of the stratum that *has* a discard observation |
| `discards` | total discards, tonnes |
| `coverage` | `landings_with_discards / landings * 100` — the share of landings backed by a discard observation |
| `discard_rate` | `discards / (landings_with_discards + discards)` |
| `stratum_id` | the dims pasted with `" | "`. This is the key `catchRaising()` conditions are written against. |

Note what `coverage` is not: it is not the share of trips sampled. It is
the share of *landings* that sit in a part of the stratum where discards
were observed. That is the quantity that matters for whether a raising is
defensible.

Then attach a status:

```{r}
strata <- classify_strata(strata, threshold = 50)
```

| argument | what to put in it |
|---|---|
| `threshold` | coverage percentage at or above which a stratum is treated as sufficiently sampled. 50 is a common starting point, not a rule. |
| `what` | `"discard"` (default), or `"length"` / `"age"` for biology coverage, which classifies on coverage **and** number of measurements. |
| `min_meas` | only for `"length"`/`"age"`: measurements below this count as insufficient however good the coverage looks. A stratum with 99% coverage and 11 fish measured should not be green. |

## 3. Exploring, with a filter {#exploring-with-a-filter}

This is where you decide how to group, so it is worth doing properly.

```{r}
plot_coverage(strata, type = "heatmap", y = "metier4", fill = "ICESDivision")
plot_discard_rate(strata, type = "box", x = "metier4")
```

In the app the filter sits **beside the axis pickers on each figure tab**,
so the loop is: put `metier4` on the Y axis, see the spread, pin
`metier4` to `TBB`, look again. Each tab owns its filter — pinning the
coverage figure leaves the discard-rate figure alone — and none of them
touch the grouping or the raising.

Here, subset the **catches**, not the strata, and rebuild:

```{r}
explore_data <- apply_filters(catch_data, list(metier4 = "TBB"))

explore_strata <- classify_strata(build_strata(explore_data, dims), 50)
plot_discard_rate(explore_strata, type = "box", x = "ICESDivision")
```

`apply_filters()` combines columns with AND and values within a column
with OR — "beam trawl, in either of these two divisions":

```{r}
apply_filters(catch_data,
              list(metier4 = "TBB", ICESDivision = c("27.4.b", "27.4.c")))
```

Naming a column that is not in the table is an **error**, not a silent
pass. A figure that looks filtered and is not is the worst possible input
to a grouping decision.

Two helpers make the filter honest rather than just convenient:

```{r}
explore_filter_levels(catch_data)         # what can usefully be filtered
filter_coverage(catch_data, list(metier4 = "TBB"))
```

`explore_filter_levels()` offers only columns that are present and have
more than one value — a filter that cannot change the figure is not worth
a dropdown. `filter_coverage()` reports rows kept **and weight kept**,
because a filter can easily keep 40% of the rows and 2% of the landings,
and a figure drawn on 2% of the landings is not a view of the fleet.

```{r}
filter_label(list(metier4 = "TBB"))   # "metier4 = TBB", for subtitles
```

In the app the same filter is a panel on the Data tab. It narrows the
coverage, discard-rate, numbers-at-length/age and mean-weight figures and
**nothing else**; the grouping and raising below always run on the full
table, and a banner says so while a filter is on.

## 4. Defining groups

A "group" is a set of strata that will be raised together, plus the pool
of strata whose data does the raising. Two ways to arrive at one. Both
return the same object, so the raising step does not care which you used.

### Automatic — a cascade

Each stratum gets the *first* donor pool that clears its threshold: its
own data if that is covered enough, else the narrowest wider pool that
qualifies, else everything.

```{r}
groups <- define_raising_groups_auto(
  strata,
  hierarchy      = c("metier4", "ICESDivision", "Season"),
  thresholds     = c(50, 40, 30),
  self_threshold = 60,
  dims           = dims)
```

| argument | what to put in it |
|---|---|
| `hierarchy` | the widening keys, **finest first**. Step 1 groups on all of them, the last step on the first one alone. |
| `thresholds` | one number, or one per hierarchy level. Falling numbers are the normal shape: you accept less coverage as you are forced to widen. |
| `self_threshold` | coverage at which a stratum raises on its own data and never enters the cascade. `NA` folds this into the first step. |
| `dims` | the full stratum dimensions. Defaults to `hierarchy`; pass it explicitly when the strata are finer than the cascade keys, which is the usual case. |
| `all_label` | label for the final catch-all pool. Leave it. |

Inspect before you commit:

```{r}
groups$summary                 # one row per group: level, condition, n strata
plot_river(groups$strata)      # which strata resolved at which step
```

### Manual — explicit rules

When the cascade cannot express the decision — "these three metiers raise
together because the WG said so" — write the rules out.

A **rule** is a list with an `id`, a `raise` side (which strata this rule
raises) and a `donor` side (whose data does the raising). Each side is a
list of clauses, and a clause is `var` + `values` (or `set`), optionally
negated:

```{r}
rules <- list(
  list(id    = "beam_trawl",
       raise = list(list(var = "metier4", values = "TBB")),
       donor = list(list(var = "metier4", values = c("TBB", "TBB_DEF")))),
  list(id    = "everything_else",
       raise = list(),          # no clause = every remaining stratum
       donor = list(list(var = "ICESDivision", values = "27.4.b")))
)

groups <- define_raising_groups_manual(strata, rules)
```

**Rules are first-match-wins.** A rule with an empty `raise` claims every
stratum, but only *receives* the ones no earlier rule took. The package
writes the complements out explicitly when it builds the conditions, so
what `catchRaising()` gets is a genuine partition — it rejects anything
that double-assigns a stratum.

### Keeping strata out of a donor pool

A stratum that is itself barely sampled is a poor donor: raising a
neighbour on it lends the neighbour a rate resting on very little. Three
routes, all reaching the same place — a set of stratum keys:

```{r}
exclusion_choices(strata, dims, order_by = "coverage")   # what to pick from
excluded_keys(strata, dims,
              named    = "TBB | 27.4.c",   # expert judgement
              cov_min  = 40,               # coverage bar
              meas_min = 30,               # measurement bar (biology)
              dr_min   = 0.02, dr_max = 0.8)
exclusion_overview(strata, dims, cov_min = 40)  # and why each one is out
```

`exclusion_choices()` labels carry the numbers the decision is made on —
coverage, discard rate, measurements, weight — so the list can be read
and acted on without a table beside it. Order it by `"coverage"` to put
the thinnest strata, the likeliest candidates, at the top.

Why the thresholds resolve to keys rather than staying as expressions:
the condition handed to `catchRaising()` is evaluated against **CEF
rows**, and those carry no `coverage` column — coverage is a property of
a stratum, computed from many rows. So a bar is applied here, against the
stratum table, and emitted as an explicit list. Whatever the route, the
engine receives a plain `!paste(...) %in% c(...)`.

Feed it to the cascade:

```{r}
strata <- flag_donor_exclusion(strata, cov_min = 40,
                               excluded = excluded_keys(strata, dims,
                                                        cov_min = 40),
                               dims = dims)
```

**Exclusion narrows the donor pool only.** It never removes a stratum
from what is raised or allocated — a stratum too thin to lend its data is
exactly the one that most needs to borrow.

For the biology groups, the same keys fold into `bioMatchedCond`:

```{r}
alloc_matched_cond(list(catchCategory = "Dis"),
                   excluded = excluded_keys(bio_link, dims, meas_min = 30),
                   dims = dims)
```

### The catch-all

The last group in a manual set carries no clause, so it claims whatever
no earlier group claimed. It has **its own** exclusion bars rather than
inheriting the ones above: a stratum kept out of one group's pool is
usually still wanted as a last resort, but one with almost nothing
measured is a bad donor everywhere. Both builders offer the same control,
plus a tick-box to inherit the group exclusions as well.

`sets` lets a list of values be named once and reused:

```{r}
sets <- list(north = c("27.4.a", "27.4.b"))
rules <- list(list(id = "north", raise = list(list(var = "ICESDivision",
                                                  set = "north")),
                   donor = list()))
groups <- define_raising_groups_manual(strata, rules, sets = sets)
```

### What both produce

```{r}
groups$strataCond        # named list of quosures: which strata each group raises
groups$matchedDataCond   # named list of quosures: which strata donate
```

That pair is the entire interface to the raising and allocation engines.
Anything that produces it will work, including something you write
yourself.

## 5. Raising discards

```{r}
catch_raised <- catchRaising(
  catch_data,
  condition_raising_st_list  = groups$strataCond,
  condition_matched_data_list = groups$matchedDataCond,
  type         = "discards",
  originType   = "WGEstimate",
  variableType = "WeightLive")
```

| argument | what to put in it |
|---|---|
| `type` | `"discards"` for the normal case. |
| `originType` | the origin label written onto the raised rows. `"WGEstimate"` is the convention for a working-group estimate. |
| `variableType` | the weight variable being raised. `"WeightLive"` unless you know otherwise. |
| `log_file` | path for the run log. Worth setting; it records what raised what. |

`run_native_raising()` is a thin wrapper that checks the CEF table has the
columns `catchRaising()` needs before calling it, and returns a readable
error instead of a stack trace when it does not:

```{r}
cef_check(catch_data)$missing
catch_raised <- run_native_raising(catch_data, dims, groups,
                                   type = "discards",
                                   log_file = "raising_log.txt")
```

## 6. Length and age

The distributions table is the second input. Prepare it, then check it
actually links to the strata you are about to allocate over.

```{r}
dist <- prep_distributions(dist_data, type = "LengthTotal")
link <- link_dist_to_strata(catch_data, dist_data, dims,
                            catch_category = "Dis", type = "LengthTotal")
```

> **The one trap in the whole pipeline.** `catchAllocationAoL()` matches
> `distributionType` against `c("Age", "Length")`, but CEF files write
> `"LengthTotal"`. The column must be rewritten to `"Length"` before the
> call. `run_allocation()` does this for you; if you call
> `catchAllocationAoL()` directly, do it yourself.

Groups are defined the same way as for discards — same two conditions,
built on biology coverage rather than discard coverage:

```{r}
bio_strata <- classify_strata(build_strata(catch_data, dims),
                              threshold = 50, what = "length", min_meas = 30)

bio_groups <- define_raising_groups_auto(
  bio_strata,
  hierarchy  = c("metier4", "ICESDivision"),
  thresholds = c(50, 40),
  dims       = dims)
```

#### Landings and discards, held to different standards

Discards are sampled less than landings almost everywhere. A single
coverage bar therefore either lets landings resolve on too little data or
pushes every discard stratum to the bottom rung. The biology cascade takes
its thresholds as a **pair**:

```{r}
steps <- alloc_steps(
  keys       = c("metier4", "ICESDivision"),
  thresholds = list(Lan = c(60, 50, 40), Dis = c(30, 25, 20)),
  min_meas   = list(Lan = c(100, 50, 30), Dis = c(20, 10, 10)),
  keep_cc    = TRUE)

assigned <- assign_alloc_cascade(bio_link, alloc_cols, steps)
```

| shape | meaning |
|---|---|
| `50` | one bar, both categories, every rung |
| `c(50, 40, 30)` | one bar per rung, both categories |
| `list(Lan = ..., Dis = ...)` | a bar per rung, per category |

All three are accepted, so a scenario saved before the split still loads.

Two things worth knowing about how the pair is read:

* **The bar belongs to the stratum being allocated, not to the pool it
  draws on.** A discard stratum keeps its looser bar even at a rung where
  `keep_cc = FALSE` has joined the categories and the pool now holds
  landings too.
* **BMS follows discards**, matching `bms_as_dis` elsewhere.

A pool must clear *both* bars: enough coverage **and** enough measured
fish. A pool can easily reach 80% coverage on eleven fish, and that is not
a distribution anyone should allocate from.

#### Strata with no catch

A stratum whose weight is zero has nothing to allocate. It can never clear
a coverage test — the denominator is zero — so it is taken out **before**
the ladder runs, labelled `"no catch to allocate"`, and reported on its
own row rather than in the unresolved list. Left in, it would send you
loosening thresholds to chase strata that need nothing.

```{r}
table(assigned$alloc_level)
subset(assigned, alloc_empty)      # the ones that needed no resolution
```

Then allocate:

```{r}
alloc <- run_allocation(
  catch_raised, dist_data, bio_groups,
  app_type           = "LengthTotal",   # or "Age"
  originType_catch   = "WGEstimate",
  variableType_catch = "WeightLive",
  variableType_mean  = "WeightLive",
  weighting          = "NumberAtAoL")
```

| argument | what to put in it |
|---|---|
| `app_type` | `"LengthTotal"` or `"Age"`. This is the app-side name; the translation to what the engine wants happens inside. |
| `originType_catch`, `variableType_catch` | must match what the raising wrote, or the allocation finds nothing to allocate over. |
| `variableType_mean` | the variable the mean weights are in. |
| `weighting` | how the donor distributions are combined. `"NumberAtAoL"` weights by numbers. |

Then aggregate. Note that the aggregation functions return **wide** tables
with the class in the column name (`N_Length_2900`), so a plot needs a
`pivot_longer` first — `agg_numbers()` and `agg_meanweight()` handle that:

```{r}
numbers_at <- agg_numbers(alloc,
                          grouping  = c("catchCategory", "sampledOrEstimated"),
                          minAoL    = 0,
                          maxAoL    = NA,
                          plusGroup = FALSE,
                          unit      = NULL,
                          round     = 2)

weights_at <- agg_meanweight(alloc,
                             grouping = c("catchCategory", "sampledOrEstimated"))
```

| argument | what to put in it |
|---|---|
| `grouping` | columns the output is broken down by. `catchCategory` splits landings from discards; `sampledOrEstimated` splits what was measured from what was allocated. |
| `minAoL`, `maxAoL` | class range to keep. `NA` for no upper bound. |
| `plusGroup` | `TRUE` accumulates everything at or above `maxAoL` into one class. |
| `unit` | output unit for the classes; `NULL` leaves them as they are. |

## 7. Getting the script back out

The app writes this sequence for the session you ran, as a single script
or as an ICES TAF script set. Two things about what it writes are worth
knowing:

**Only saved allocations are written.** The on-screen configuration is
not, unless nothing at all has been saved — in which case it is written
and clearly labelled as unsaved. This keeps a script from opening with a
near-duplicate of the first saved block, which left a reader unable to
tell which one produced the numbers.

**The exploration filter is written as a separate object.** The script
gets `explore_data <- catch_data %>% filter(...)`, never an overwrite of
`catch_data`, so it stays visible on the page that the figures were drawn
on a subset and the raising was not.

```{r}
emit_explore_filter_code(list(metier4 = "TBB"))
```

## Where things are

| you want | look at |
|---|---|
| the workbench functions | `R/rcef_*.R` |
| plots and theme | `R/viz_*.R` |
| `catchRaising()`, `catchAllocationAoL()`, the CEF readers | `R/RDBESStockCoord_*.R` — vendored ICES working-group code, not modified here |
| the app | `inst/app/`, launched by `run_app()` |

The vendored files keep upstream's function names, argument lists and
return shapes exactly. Local changes are packaging-only and every one is
marked `## [pkg]`, so `grep -rn '## \[pkg\]' R/` is a complete diff
against upstream.
